ecstatic-dance.title: Ecstatic dance in London
intro: Ecstatic dance is a freeform dance floor with no talking, no alcohol and no steps to learn. A DJ builds a wave from slow and grounded to fast and loud and back down again, and everyone moves however their body wants to for a couple of hours.
London has one most nights of the week, from sunrise sessions to Friday and Saturday floors of two hundred people. Many open with cacao or a short warm-up circle and close with a lie-down.
faq: What is ecstatic dance?

A sober, freeform dance practice: no choreography, no conversation on the floor, and no drinking. The DJ's set is arranged as a journey through tempos so the room moves together without anyone leading. It grew out of the 5Rhythms and conscious dance scenes of the 1970s and 80s.
Do I need to be able to dance?
No. There is nothing to get right and nobody is watching — most people dance with their eyes half closed. Walking, stretching or lying down at the edge of the room all count.
What are the rules at an ecstatic dance?

Three, almost everywhere: no talking on the dance floor, no shoes, and no alcohol or drugs. Dancing with someone else is welcome but always invited rather than assumed — a hand raised palm-out is the usual way to decline, and it isn't taken personally.

5rhythms.title: 5Rhythms classes in London
intro: 5Rhythms is a moving meditation created by Gabrielle Roth: every class travels through flowing, staccato, chaos, lyrical and stillness, a wave that takes about two hours. A teacher holds the room and offers a focus, but there are no steps to copy.
London has one of the largest 5Rhythms communities anywhere, with weekly classes across the city, monthly longer waves and regular weekend workshops. Drop in to any class marked open level.
faq: What are the five rhythms?

Flowing (continuous, circular, grounded), staccato (defined, rhythmic, expressive), chaos (letting go of control), lyrical (light and playful) and stillness (settling, breath). Danced in sequence they make a wave, the basic form of every class.
Is 5Rhythms suitable for beginners?
Yes — most weekly classes are open level and a good share of the room is new. There is no technique to learn and no partner needed; the teacher's instructions are invitations rather than steps.
How is 5Rhythms different from ecstatic dance?
5Rhythms is a taught practice with a fixed map and certified teachers who guide the room through the wave. Ecstatic dance is usually DJ-led and unguided. Both are sober, barefoot and freeform.

sound-bath.title: Sound baths, gong baths & sound healing in London
intro: A sound bath is an hour lying on the floor while someone plays gongs, singing bowls, chimes and voice around the room. There is nothing to do: the sound is long and overlapping, and most people drift between waking and sleep.
London's sound baths run in yoga studios, churches and railway arches, often in the early evening. Bring warm socks — you cool down quickly lying still — and expect to leave slightly dazed.

You'll also see them billed as sound healing, sound meditation, sound journeys or vibrational sound therapy: in a group setting these are all much the same thing, led with gongs, crystal and Tibetan singing bowls, chimes, drums and voice. Many people come for the rest itself — to switch off, sleep better or let go of a stressful week.
faq: What is a sound bath?

A group session where you lie down and listen to sustained acoustic sound — usually gongs and crystal or Tibetan bowls — for forty-five to sixty minutes. 'Bath' refers to being surrounded by sound, not to water; nothing is asked of you beyond lying still.
What should I bring to a sound bath?

Warm layers and socks, and a blanket if the listing doesn't say one is provided. Most venues supply mats, bolsters and eye masks. Arrive early enough to settle, as latecomers are often held at the door once the gongs start.
Is a gong bath the same as a sound bath?

A gong bath is a sound bath led mainly by gongs, which are louder and more physical than bowls — you feel them in your chest. Sessions billed as sound healing or sound journeys use a wider mix of instruments and often voice.
What's the difference between a sound bath and sound therapy?

A sound bath is a group session: everyone lies down and the practitioner plays for the room. Sound therapy usually means a one-to-one treatment, such as a singing bowl massage where bowls are placed on or around your body. Group sessions are cheaper and need no booking ahead beyond a ticket; this page lists the group ones.
How long is a sound bath?

Most London sound baths last 45 to 75 minutes of sound, with time either side to settle in and come round — so allow an hour and a half. Lunchtime and early-morning sessions can be as short as half an hour, and all-night gong journeys run until dawn.
Can a sound bath help with sleep and stress?

Many people find them deeply relaxing and sleep well afterwards, and small studies have reported lower tension and better mood after a session. They aren't a medical treatment, but as an hour of enforced rest with no screen and nothing to do, they work for a lot of people.

cacao-ceremony.title: Cacao ceremonies & cacao circles in London
intro: A cacao ceremony is a gathering where everyone drinks a cup of thick, bitter ceremonial cacao together and then sits, moves or shares for a couple of hours. The cacao is a mild heart opener, not a psychedelic: it lifts the mood, warms the chest and makes people a little more willing to be honest with each other.

In London they usually run on a weekday evening or a Sunday afternoon, often paired with ecstatic dance, sound, breathwork or a sharing circle. Expect two to three hours, a room of twenty to eighty people, and no requirement to say anything at all.
faq: What happens at a cacao ceremony?

You arrive, sit in a circle and are handed a cup of ceremonial cacao — thick, dark and unsweetened. The facilitator usually opens with an intention or a short meditation while the cacao takes effect over twenty minutes or so, then leads whatever the evening is built around: dance, sound, breathwork, journalling or open sharing. Most end with a closing circle.
Is cacao a drug, and is it safe?

Ceremonial cacao is food, not a drug — it's unprocessed cacao with theobromine and a little caffeine, so it feels like a strong coffee with a warmer edge. It's worth telling the facilitator beforehand if you take antidepressants (particularly MAOIs), have a heart condition, or are pregnant, as they will often serve a smaller dose.
Can I go to a cacao ceremony on my own?
Yes — most people there came alone. Facilitators build in introductions and pairs, and nobody is made to speak or touch anyone. Arriving ten minutes early makes the first circle easier.
What is ceremonial cacao?

Whole cacao beans, fermented, roasted, shelled and ground into a paste with nothing taken out — unlike cocoa powder, which has the fat removed, or chocolate, which is mostly sugar. A ceremonial cup is about 20–40g melted into hot water, sometimes with chilli, cinnamon or a little sweetener. Most London facilitators source it from Guatemala, Peru or Ecuador.
What should I do before a cacao ceremony?

Eat lightly beforehand — cacao is rich and sits better on a half-empty stomach — and skip coffee that day, as the two together can feel jittery. Wear something comfortable you can sit on the floor or dance in, and bring water.
Where are cacao ceremonies held in London?

In yoga studios, community halls, churches and wellbeing centres across the city, with the most in east and north London. Many are the opening of an ecstatic dance or a sound bath; the listings above say what each evening is built around.

breathwork.title: Breathwork classes & workshops in London
intro: Breathwork is a session where a facilitator guides you through a specific breathing pattern — usually connected, mouth-led and faster than normal — while you lie down with music playing. Thirty to sixty minutes of it can bring tingling, strong emotion, tears or a deep calm, and the session closes with rest and sharing.
London runs everything from lunchtime classes to weekend intensives, in styles from gentle and somatic to the intense holotropic lineage. Most are two hours and need no experience.
Weekly community classes are the easiest way in, in east London especially; ceremonies pair the breath with cacao, live sound or dance, and there are men's, women's and partner sessions too.
faq: What happens in a breathwork session?

You lie on a mat with an eye mask while the facilitator talks you into a connected breathing rhythm — in through the mouth, no pause at the top, out with a release. After twenty to forty minutes of active breathing the music softens and you rest, then the group usually shares what came up.
Is breathwork safe?

For most people, yes, though tingling hands and a tight jaw are common and harmless. Facilitators normally ask you to check in first if you have epilepsy, cardiovascular problems, glaucoma, severe asthma, a history of psychosis, or are pregnant — the faster styles aren't recommended in those cases.
Do I need any experience?
No. Almost every London session is open to first-timers and the facilitator explains the pattern before anything starts. You can stop and breathe normally whenever you want.
What types of breathwork are there?

Conscious connected breathwork (the most common in London: continuous breathing with no pause) and its forerunner rebirthing; holotropic and neurodynamic breathwork, longer and more intense, done with evocative music, often in pairs; shamanic breathwork, which adds drumming and ritual; and gentler slow or coherent breathing for calm. Wim Hof's method is a breathwork style too, usually paired with cold exposure.
What should I wear and bring to breathwork?

Loose, warm clothes — you lie still for a long time and can get cold — and water for afterwards. Eat lightly, at least an hour or two before. Mats, blankets and eye masks are usually provided; the listing will say if not.

somatics.title: Somatic workshops & embodiment in London
intro: Somatic work starts from the body rather than the story: slow movement, attention to sensation, and pauses long enough to notice what shifts. It's used for trauma, stress and plain disconnection, and looks far less dramatic than it feels.

London's somatic scene spans trauma-informed workshops, Feldenkrais classes, embodiment labs and movement research. Most sessions are small, and touch — where it happens at all — is always asked for first.
faq: What does somatic mean?

Somatic simply means 'of the body'. In practice it describes approaches that work through felt sensation and movement rather than talk alone — noticing where you brace, letting a movement finish, following what the nervous system does next.
Is somatic work therapy?

Some of it is: somatic experiencing and similar modalities are clinical approaches delivered by trained practitioners. Group workshops and embodiment classes are educational rather than therapeutic, though they often touch the same ground.
Will I have to be touched?
Not unless you choose to be. Most London sessions are solo or guided in pairs with explicit consent, and 'I'd rather not' is a complete answer.

qigong.title: Qigong classes in London
intro: Qigong is a Chinese practice of slow, repeated movement coordinated with breath and attention. Sequences are short and undramatic — standing, shifting weight, opening and closing the arms — and are meant to be repeated rather than perfected.
London classes run in parks, community halls and studios, often early morning, and many are drop-in. Come in clothes you can move in; nothing more is needed.
faq: What is qigong?

A practice from Chinese medicine combining gentle movement, breathing and focused attention, usually done standing. Where tai chi is a long martial form, qigong is a set of short repeatable exercises.
Is qigong suitable for beginners or older people?
Yes — it's low impact, done standing or seated, and can be scaled to almost any level of mobility. Most London classes are mixed ability and welcome complete beginners.
What should I wear to a qigong class?
Loose, warm clothing and flat shoes, or bare feet indoors. Outdoor classes carry on in most weather, so dress for standing still in it.

tantra.title: Tantra workshops & classes in London
intro: Tantra workshops in London are mostly neo-tantra: a modern, Western take on the Indian tradition that works with breath, slow touch, eye contact and attention to build intimacy — with yourself, a partner or a room of strangers. An evening usually mixes guided exercises in pairs with talks on desire, boundaries and energy.

Formats run from two-hour introductions and masterclasses to women's and couples' days, tantric slow dating and full weekends. Clothes stay on at almost all of them; the few that differ say so clearly on the listing.
faq: What happens at a tantra workshop?

Most begin in a circle with an introduction and some breath or movement to settle the room. Then come exercises, often in pairs: eye gazing, synchronised breathing, giving and receiving simple touch on the hands or back, and practising asking for what you want and saying no. They close with sharing.
Do I need a partner, and is it sexual?

No partner is needed — most people come alone, and you can sit out any exercise. Introductory workshops are clothed and non-sexual; they work with sexual energy as a theme, not as an activity. Consent is taught explicitly, and every exercise is an invitation you can decline.
Is tantra a religion?

Classical tantra is a family of Hindu and Buddhist traditions with long lineages. The London workshops are neo-tantra, which borrows some practices and language from them but asks for no belief — closer to a relationship or embodiment class than to a religious rite.

family-constellations.title: Family constellations workshops in London
intro: Family constellations is a group process developed by Bert Hellinger. One person brings an issue — usually about family, relationships or a repeating pattern — and chooses people from the room to stand in for family members. Placed in space, the representatives often feel and say surprising things, and the facilitator works with what shows up.

London workshops run as evenings and full days, often with three to six constellations set up in a session. You can come to bring an issue of your own or just to represent; the listing usually says which places are left.
faq: What happens in a family constellations workshop?

The group sits in a circle. Someone with an issue tells the facilitator briefly what it is, then picks representatives for themselves and the people involved and places them in the room. The representatives report what they sense, and the facilitator moves people and offers sentences until the picture settles. Each constellation takes thirty to sixty minutes.
Do I have to bring an issue?

No. Many people come as participants only, representing in other people's constellations, which is how most people learn what the work is like. Bringing an issue is often priced higher and booked ahead.
Is family constellations therapy?

It's used alongside therapy but isn't a regulated treatment, and the evidence for it is limited. It can bring up strong feelings, so look for experienced facilitators, and tell them beforehand if you are in crisis or recently bereaved.

authentic-relating.title: Authentic relating & circling in London
intro: Authentic relating is a set of guided conversation practices for meeting people honestly: saying what is actually true for you in the moment, and getting curious about the person in front of you instead of performing. Evenings are a sequence of games in pairs and small groups, each with a simple structure and a facilitator holding time.

Circling is its deeper sibling: a group of five to ten turns its whole attention on one person, or on the group itself, and reflects back what it notices. London has weekly drop-ins, beginner evenings and full circling weekends.
faq: What happens at an authentic relating evening?

After a short welcome you're paired up for structured games — one person asks a question, the other answers, then you swap, or you take turns finishing a sentence like "right now I notice…". The structures make it easy to go past small talk quickly. Expect plenty of rotation and a sharing circle at the end.
What is circling?

A group practice in which everyone gives their attention to one person's experience in the moment — what they feel, how they're landing with the group — and says what they notice in return. It's slower and more intimate than relating games, and usually led by a trained facilitator.
Is it therapy?
No. It's a social practice, not treatment, and nobody is asked to dig into their history. You choose how much to share, and "I'd rather not say" is a welcome answer.

contact-improvisation.title: Contact improvisation jams & classes in London
intro: Contact improvisation is a movement practice built on a shared point of contact: two people lean, roll, lift and give weight, following momentum rather than choreography. It's danced barefoot and usually in silence or to quiet music.
London has weekly jams — open floors where anyone can dance with anyone — plus classes for people who want the technique first. Jams often ask for some prior experience; classes never do.
faq: What is contact improvisation?

A duet form developed by Steve Paxton in the 1970s in which dancers share weight through a moving point of contact. Nothing is set in advance: the dance follows physics — momentum, gravity and the surface between two bodies.
Is contact improv a beginner-friendly practice?

Classes are, and are the right place to start: you learn rolling, giving weight and how to keep each other safe. Open jams assume you already have those basics, so check the listing before turning up to one.
Is contact improvisation intimate?
It involves a lot of physical contact but is not romantic or sexual, and consent is explicit throughout — you can decline a dance or end one at any point without explanation.

bohm-dialogue.title: Bohm dialogue groups in London
intro: A Bohm dialogue is a group conversation with no agenda, no leader and nothing to decide. Ten to forty people sit in a circle and talk, and the practice is to notice your own assumptions and reactions as they arise — to hold them up for the group to look at rather than defend them.

It comes from the physicist David Bohm, who saw thought as a collective process and dialogue as a way of watching it work. London groups usually meet for two to three hours on a weekday evening or weekend afternoon, often opening with a short introduction for newcomers.
faq: What happens in a Bohm dialogue?

The group sits in a circle and a facilitator opens the space, sometimes with a theme or a reading, then steps back. Anyone can speak; there is no turn-taking and no goal to reach. Long silences are normal, and the facilitator may pause the room to reflect on what the conversation itself is doing.
How is it different from a debate or a discussion group?

A debate tries to win and a discussion tries to reach a conclusion. A Bohm dialogue does neither: the aim is to suspend judgement — your own as much as anyone's — and see the shared assumptions underneath what people say.
Do I need to have read Bohm first?

No. Introductory sessions explain the principles at the start, and most groups welcome people who've never heard of it. If you want to read ahead, Bohm's short book On Dialogue is the usual starting point.

kirtan.title: Kirtan & chanting circles in London
intro: Kirtan is call-and-response chanting from the Indian devotional tradition: a leader sings a line of a mantra, usually with harmonium and drum, and the room sings it back, slowly at first and then faster until it lifts. Nobody needs to sing well, and the words are simple and repeated.
London's chanting circles also cover Vedic chanting, mantra circles and Celtic and devotional song. Most are an evening of ninety minutes to two hours, seated on cushions or chairs.
faq: What happens at a kirtan?

You sit in a circle or rows facing the musicians. The leader introduces a mantra and what it means, sings each line, and everyone answers. Each chant builds over ten to twenty minutes, and there's usually silence between them. Song sheets are often handed out.
Do I need to be religious or able to sing?
No. The mantras come from Hindu devotion, but London kirtans welcome people of any faith or none, and the point is joining in rather than singing well. You can also just listen.

shamanic.title: Shamanic journeys, drumming & trance dance in London
intro: Shamanic sessions use rhythm, breath and ritual to reach an altered, dreamlike state without substances. The classic form is the drum journey: you lie down with eyes covered while a steady drumbeat, around four beats a second, carries you into a guided inner journey.

In London the word covers drum circles and journeying groups, shamanic breathwork, and blindfolded trance dance, where you move freely under a blindfold to drums and deep bass. Most sessions are open to beginners and close with sharing.
faq: What is a shamanic drum journey?

A guided meditation carried by repetitive drumming. You lie down, set an intention, and follow the drum into an inner landscape for fifteen to thirty minutes until a change of rhythm calls you back. Many people experience vivid imagery; others simply rest deeply. Nothing is taken: the rhythm does the work.
What is trance dance?

A blindfolded dance practice: wearing a scarf over your eyes, you move to drumming or bass-heavy music, breathing deeply, and let the movement take over. Helpers keep the space safe so nobody collides. Sessions often open with breathwork and end lying down.

sufi-whirling.title: Sufi whirling & Sufi meditation in London
intro: Sufi whirling, or turning, is the moving meditation of the Mevlevi order founded after the 13th-century poet Rumi: you turn slowly on the spot, right hand raised and left lowered, keeping a still centre as the room spins around you. Classes start very slowly, and turning is learned over months rather than one night.
London has regular turning practices and classes, Sema ceremonies open to watch, and Sufi meditation groups that work with breath, repeated sacred phrases (dhikr) and silent sitting.
faq: Do you get dizzy whirling?

Beginners usually do at first. Teachers start with only a few turns, with your gaze resting softly on your raised hand or unfocused, and build up gradually; with practice the dizziness fades and the turning becomes calm.
Do I need to be Muslim to learn Sufi whirling?
No. The practice comes from the Mevlevi Sufi tradition within Islam, and teachers treat it with respect, but London classes and meditation groups welcome people of any faith or none.
